bull_thesis: YETI is a genuinely good business that just proved its operating turn is real, and the market is only starting to pay for it. Three facts carry the case. First, pricing power never broke: gross margin (revenue left after the cost of making the product) was 57.8% in 2021 and is 57.0% on a trailing twelve-month basis today, held intact through a tariff regime that management sized at roughly $0.35 per share of added cost in 2025 and a similar amount again in 2026, and through what they called a highly promotional drinkware market. A brand that can hold a 57% gross margin while a whole category discounts around it is not losing its customer. Second, the growth is back and it is broad. Drinkware, 58% of sales, has now grown for two consecutive quarters (up 6% in the fourth quarter of 2025, up 5% in the first quarter of 2026 with both sell-in to retailers and sell-through to consumers growing in the US) after a year of decline; coolers and equipment grew double digits on soft coolers and bags; global wholesale grew 19% in the first quarter of 2026, described on the 14 May 2026 call as the strongest wholesale quarter in more than three years; and international is compounding above 20% and heading toward 23%-plus of full-year sales. Management raised full-year 2026 guidance on 14 May 2026 to 7-8% sales growth and $2.83-$2.89 of adjusted earnings per share, up from 6-8% and $2.77-$2.83. Third, the capital return is doing real work: $307.8 million of stock was repurchased in the trailing twelve months to April 2026, about 8% of the current $3.84 billion market value, taking the diluted share count from 84.9 million in late 2024 to 76.7 million. Free cash flow of $216 million exceeds net income of $159 million by 1.9 times, and net debt is only $97 million including capitalised leases. On top of that sits a credibility record that argues the published guidance is a floor: seven consecutive quarterly earnings beats, including $0.26 adjusted against a $0.18 consensus in the first quarter of 2026, and a specific dated promise made in August 2025 that drinkware would return to growth in the fourth quarter, which it did on schedule. The upside lever nobody is modelling is operating leverage. Selling, general and administrative costs have climbed from 38.4% of revenue in 2021 to 46.0% in fiscal 2025, funding five product-design offices (Austin, Bozeman, Denver, Thailand, Vietnam), the largest brand campaigns in company history, a Japan build-out and a run of design and tooling acquisitions. If even two of those seven-plus points come back as the supply chain settles and international matures, adjusted earnings power moves toward $3.50 rather than $2.86, and the stock re-rates on both the earnings and the multiple. The conditions this case needs: drinkware growth must hold above 4-5% through the second half; the tariff rate must not step up from the roughly 20% baked into guidance (and the proposed replacement tariff architecture at 10-12.5% would be a tailwind if it lands there); and the second-half gross-margin recovery management promised on the 14 May 2026 call must actually appear.
bear_thesis: Strip away the narrative and this is a company that has grown revenue 32% since 2021 and earns less money than it did then. Net income fell from $213 million in 2021 to $159 million on a trailing twelve-month basis, a 25% decline. Diluted earnings per share went from $2.40 to $1.96 even after retiring 13% of the shares. Five-year earnings-per-share growth is negative 4.1% a year. Because gross margin is flat at 57%, all of that damage sits in operating spending, which has absorbed 7.6 percentage points of revenue since 2021. Across five consecutive earnings calls, no analyst asked and no executive volunteered a date or a number for when that spend converts into margin. The one analyst who came closest (November 2025, on whether investors should expect operating-expense leverage in the out years) received an answer containing neither. The bear case is simply that the answer is never: that the five design offices, the 400-million-impression campaigns, the Japan and China entries and the acquisition-led product pipeline are not a temporary investment hump but the new permanent cost of defending a brand in a category with almost no barrier to entry. The competitive evidence supports that reading. Management has never once named a competitor across five calls, referring only to the market, some brands out there, and certain trend-driven styles going promotional; that is a company describing share loss without saying to whom. Insulated drinkware is a fashion-adjacent category, and YETI needed a full year of category cleanup plus a portfolio redefinition (into cookware, tableware, barware and shaker bottles) to get drinkware back to 5-6% growth. The first quarter of 2026 shows what that growth costs: revenue up 8% but reported earnings per share down 35% year over year, $0.13 on a generally-accepted basis against $0.26 adjusted. The 19% wholesale surge is also the least durable part of the quarter, since retailer restocking after a year of destocking is a one-time catch-up, not a run rate, and management themselves said in February 2026 that they were not planning for a significant inflection. What confirms the bear: a second-half where gross margin does not recover as promised, or drinkware slipping back toward flat, or wholesale growth decelerating sharply off the restock comparison. # YETI Holdings (NYSE: YETI) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared from five consecutive quarterly earnings calls (May 2025 through May 2026) cross-referenced against the screener's financial trajectory and live market data as of 27 July 2026. Share price used throughout: $50.72 (US dollars, NYSE close, 24 July 2026).*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story changed from survival to acceleration, and the numbers followed — but only on the top line.**

In May 2025, chief executive Matt Reintjes opened the call by naming three priorities that were unmistakably defensive: "accelerating the pace of product innovation, materially transforming our supply chain, minimizing exposure to China and delivering operating discipline to maintain our fortress balance sheet." He called 2025 "a transition year." The company was pulling production out of China at speed, deliberately delaying product launches, cutting planned capital spending, and running inventory down to limit tariff exposure. Management was explicit that its own supply-chain surgery would cost it growth: "the full impact of this innovation on our 2025 growth will be partially offset by inventory supply disruption caused by our supply chain diversification efforts."

By August 2025 the tone had darkened further on the demand side. Drinkware — then 58% of sales — was described as "highly promotional" with the market "shift[ing] away from the recent trend-driven growth," and guidance was cut. The bright spots were narrow: bags and packs, and international.

The November 2025 call was the hinge. For the first time management introduced a long-term growth framework — "a long-term top line growth range of high single to low double digits" — while the quarter itself still showed US wholesale orders falling. That is a notable sequencing choice: the ambition was raised before the evidence arrived.

Then the evidence did arrive. In February 2026 (fourth quarter of fiscal 2025), drinkware grew 6% and international grew 25%, both the best of the year; management guided 2026 to 6–8% sales growth. In May 2026 (first quarter of fiscal 2026) the company delivered 8% sales growth, wholesale up 19% — "our strongest wholesale quarter in more than 3 years" — and raised full-year guidance to 7–8% sales growth and adjusted earnings of $2.83–$2.89 per share.

**What was quietly dropped:** the phrase "fortress balance sheet" and the tariff-crisis framing largely disappeared after early 2026, replaced by "the earnings power of the model" and "compound value over time." **What was added:** a sports and fitness hydration angle, a $2.5 billion shaker-bottle market claim, an artificial-intelligence shopping assistant called Ranger, a TikTok shop, and a fourth and fifth product-design office (Thailand, then Vietnam). The company has widened its self-definition from a cooler-and-tumbler brand to an outdoor-lifestyle platform spanning bags, cookware, protective cases and sports hydration.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The central finding of this dossier is a gap that none of the five calls addresses directly: **YETI has grown revenue 32% since 2021 and earned less money per share at the end of it than at the beginning.**

| Management claim | Where said | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Our brand is connecting… long-term top line growth range of high single to low double digits" | Nov 2025 | Revenue: $1.41B (2021) to $1.87B (fiscal 2025), a 32% rise, but only +2.1% year over year in fiscal 2025 and +5.4% over three years. First quarter 2026 finally hit +8%. | **Partly supported.** The recent acceleration is real; the multi-year record is mid-single-digit, not high-single-to-low-double. |
| "Strong gross and operating margins" | recurring | Gross margin is genuinely intact: 57.8% in 2021, 57.4% in fiscal 2025, 57.0% trailing twelve months. It survived a tariff shock and a promotional holiday. | **Supported — and this is the strongest fact in the file.** Pricing power did not break. |
| "The earnings power of the model" | May 2026 | Diluted earnings per share: $2.40 (2021) to $2.03 (fiscal 2025) to $1.96 trailing twelve months. Net income fell from $213M to $159M — a 25% decline — while the share count fell 13%. Five-year earnings-per-share growth is *negative* 4.1% a year. | **Contradicted.** Earnings power has shrunk, not grown. |
| Operating discipline / cost management | recurring, esp. 2025 | Selling, general and administrative costs went from 38.4% of revenue in 2021 to 46.0% in fiscal 2025 — a 7.6 percentage-point build. Trailing operating margin is 10.8% against 21.6% earnings-before-interest-tax-depreciation-and-amortisation margin in 2021 (14.0% today). | **Contradicted as stated.** Costs were disciplined *relative to the crisis*, not in absolute terms. Because gross margin is flat, the entire profit compression sits in operating spending. |
| Capital allocation conviction: "$500 million over the last 2 years in buybacks" | Nov 2025 | Verified and larger than stated at the run rate: $307.8M of stock repurchased in the trailing twelve months to April 2026, roughly 8% of today's $3.84B market value. Diluted share count fell from 84.9M (late 2024) to 76.7M. | **Supported, emphatically.** This is the most credible claim in the file. |
| "Free cash flow of $212 million, exceeding adjusted net income" | Feb 2026 | Trailing twelve-month free cash flow $216M against net income $159M — cash conversion of 1.9 times earnings. Balance sheet: $128M cash, $72M borrowings, $153M capitalised leases. | **Supported.** Cash generation is high quality and better than the profit line. |

But first-quarter earnings per share fell 35% year over year, and the reported quarter's profit was $0.13 on a generally-accepted basis versus $0.26 adjusted. | **Supported on volume, not on profit.** The quarter's growth was bought at a margin cost. |

**Where the story is richer than the trajectory justifies:** the repeated framing of "compound value" and "earnings power." Over five years the company has compounded revenue and *de*-compounded profit. Buybacks have masked roughly half of that decline in the per-share figures.

**Where the story is poorer than the trajectory justifies:** management under-sells the gross-margin achievement. Holding a 57% gross margin through a tariff regime that added roughly $0.35 per share of cost in 2025 and a similar amount again in 2026, while a whole product category went promotional, is genuinely difficult and is the best evidence that the brand still commands a price premium.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, and steeply so from the November 2025 call onward.**

- **May 2025 — defensive.** "This unique moment in time"; "growing macroeconomic and consumer uncertainty"; "projected headwinds." Guidance was framed around what could go wrong. The dominant verbs were *protect*, *minimize*, *lower*.
- **August 2025 — defensive with a hedge.** "Top line demand in Q2 came in slightly below expectations." On the promotional environment: "it's too early to say. There's a lot moving around." The chief financial officer would not quantify third-quarter momentum: "we're not getting too specific on what we're seeing."
- **November 2025 — the turn.** "Growing momentum from consistent and strong execution"; "our product innovation pipeline has never been more robust." The long-term growth range was introduced here, unprompted by results.
- **February 2026 — confident.** "Increasing conviction in the long-term trajectory of the brand"; "our strongest quarter of the year."
- **May 2026 — offensive.** "Q1 reinforced something more fundamental about YETI, the earnings power of the model"; "why our advantages are durable and defensible." Reintjes explicitly reframed the call away from the quarter and toward "what is getting structurally better in the business."

**Specificity of guidance increased alongside confidence**, which is the healthier pattern: in 2025 management refused to quantify near-term trends; by 2026 they were giving a tightened sales range, a tightened earnings range, an international growth range (high teens to 20%), and a half-by-half gross-margin shape ("peak tariff impact in the first half with second half gross margins recovering most of the year-over-year pressure").

The one clear shift from offensive to defensive language went the other way — from cost and supply chain in 2025 back to brand, innovation and total addressable market in 2026.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High, with one significant qualification.**

The record across these five calls:

- **The 2025 guidance was cut, twice in effect.** In May 2025 management lowered the outlook, attributing it to supply constraints from the China exit. In August 2025 they cut again, this time on US drinkware market conditions. An analyst (Anna Glaessgen, May 2025) pressed exactly on this: "It feels like the majority of the sales reduction is related to a lack of inventory to be able to meet underlying demand." Management confirmed it. So the 2025 shortfall was, by their own account, partly self-inflicted and knowable in advance.
- **Every promise made about 2026 has so far been kept or beaten.** They said 90% of US drinkware capacity would be out of China by end-2025 and that 2026 would be "a much stronger position" — the first quarter of 2026 delivered 8% growth and a guidance raise. They said drinkware would "return to growth starting in Q4" (said in August 2025) — drinkware grew 6% in the fourth quarter and 5% in the first quarter of 2026. That is a specific, dated, checkable prediction that came true on schedule.
- **The beat rate corroborates.** Seven of seven quarters beaten on earnings. The most recent: $0.26 adjusted against a $0.18 consensus in the first quarter of 2026 — a 47% beat, which is a wide enough margin to suggest deliberately conservative guidance.

**Sandbagging pattern: yes, and it is now visible.** A 100% beat rate with beats of that size means the guidance floor is set low. Investors should read the published range as a floor, not a midpoint. The qualification on the score is that sandbagging cuts both ways — the same conservatism means the 2026 raise to $2.83–$2.89 of adjusted earnings may itself be beatable, which is the bull's strongest structural argument.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**Recurring question management will not answer directly: how large is the bags business?**
Brian McNamara (Canaccord Genuity, February 2026) asked plainly: "How big are bags today?" The answer: "we haven't broken it out specifically." Bags — Camino totes, Daytrip soft coolers, the Skala hike packs, Mystery Ranch — is the single most-praised growth driver across all five calls and the one number management withholds. When a company celebrates a category in every call and refuses to size it, the reasonable inference is that it is still small relative to the enthusiasm.

**The "other" category as a canary.** Joe Altobello (Raymond James, August 2025) asked whether persistent weakness in the small "other" line — which contains apparel — was "a canary in the coal mine" for brand engagement. The chief financial officer's answer was a flat denial with three different explanations offered in one paragraph (merchandising changes, marketing strategy, freight revenue accounting). Multiple simultaneous explanations for one weak line is a soft answer.

**Destocking, asked repeatedly and answered vaguely until it resolved.** From August 2025 through February 2026 analysts kept asking whether wholesale destocking was finished. The February 2026 answer — "we're not planning for a significant inflection, we do believe that there will be more aligned in 2026" — was hedged. Three months later wholesale grew 19%. Management under-promised here and was right to.

**What analysts are not pressing hard enough on:** the operating-expense build. Across five calls, not one analyst asked why selling, general and administrative costs have risen 7.6 percentage points of revenue since 2021, or when the five design offices, the largest-ever brand campaign, and the 400-million-impression spring push are expected to produce operating leverage. Anna Glaessgen came closest (November 2025), asking about "balancing the investments required to drive the innovation… versus maybe seeing some more OpEx leverage in the out year." The answer did not contain a number or a date.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Red flag — five years of revenue growth with no profit growth (2021 through fiscal 2025).** Revenue +32%, net income −25%. Every call celebrates the top line; none reconciles the bottom.

**Red flag — the unexplained chief financial officer change (February 2026 call).** Mike McMullen was thanked and Scott Bomar welcomed, with no stated reason and no transition period disclosed on the call. Brian McNamara's "Mike, I wish you the best here" suggests it was a surprise to the sell side. A finance chief departing at the exact moment a multi-year margin story is being re-underwritten deserves weight.

**Red flag — a dropped question (February 2026).** McNamara asked three questions; Bomar answered the first and third and asked him to repeat the second (whether US drinkware would grow inside the mid-single-digit drinkware guide). Reintjes cut in: "We can move to the next question, operator." The question about domestic drinkware growth was never answered.

**The category definition keeps widening, and that is a tell in both directions.** Drinkware was tumblers; by February 2026 it was "4 platforms: bottles and jugs, cups, mugs and tumblers, tableware, coffeeware, barware and containers; and finally, cookware." **Trajectory classification: STRENGTHENING.**

The operating turn is real and is corroborated by the numbers, not just the narrative: drinkware has grown for two consecutive quarters after a year of decline, wholesale posted its best quarter in three years, international is compounding above 20%, the China exit is complete and ahead of schedule, and guidance was raised in May 2026 rather than trimmed. Cash generation exceeds reported profit, and roughly 8% of the company has been retired in a year.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *the seven-and-a-half percentage points of revenue that have migrated into operating costs since 2021 have not yet produced a single dollar of incremental profit.* Gross margin is flat at 57%, so the brand is not the problem — the spending is. Five design offices, a 400-million-impression campaign, an artificial-intelligence shopping assistant, a Japan build-out and a series of design acquisitions are all being funded out of the operating line, and management has never given a date or a number for when that spend converts to margin. The bull case and the bear case both turn entirely on this one question, and the stock is priced as though the answer is already known. At $50.72 the market pays roughly 17.7 times the midpoint of guided 2026 adjusted earnings and 3.6 times trailing gross profit for a business whose earnings per share are lower than they were five years ago.

**Economic moat: NARROW, of the intangible-brand type.**

The evidence for a moat is the gross margin — 57%, essentially unchanged since 2021, defended through a tariff shock and a promotional war, with brand awareness, consideration and preference all at or near record levels and product satisfaction around 98%. Customers pay a premium and keep paying it. That is a real, measurable brand asset.

The evidence against calling it wide is equally clear. Insulated drinkware has almost no barrier to entry, and YETI lost meaningful share to newer entrants during 2023 and 2024 — the "cleanup" and "trend-driven styles" language across four consecutive calls is management describing a category where consumer preference moves faster than the moat can defend. There are no switching costs, no network effects and no regulatory protection. The coolers and bags franchise is sturdier — heritage, price-ladder coverage from the $50–$150 Daytrip up to the $200–$350 line, and genuine product reputation — but it is a product moat, not a structural one.

But the compression is entirely below the gross-profit line, and gross margin is the metric that measures competitive position. Falling returns caused by deliberate investment and a tariff regime are a capital-allocation question, not a moat question. If the gross margin ever breaks below the mid-fifties, this rating should move immediately to eroding.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** No structural force is dismantling the terminal value here. The e-commerce channel shift, which impairs mall-based retail and wholesale distributors, works *for* YETI, which sells direct through its own site, Amazon, a new TikTok shop and its own stores while wholesale reaccelerates. There is no artificial-intelligence displacement risk, no reimbursement or regulatory cliff, no energy-transition exposure. The genuine risk is cyclical and category-fashion in nature: insulated drinkware is subject to consumer trend cycles, and a discretionary premium-priced product is exposed to a weak consumer. That is a cyclical risk, not a terminal one.

**Therefore the cheapness question is moot rather than answered: there is no cheapness to classify.** This is not a fear-print and it is not a structurally shrinking base. It is a good business, correctly recognised as such by a market that has bid it to a 52-week high, trading at approximately fair value with the profit-conversion question still open.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High, with one significant qualification.**

The record across these five calls:

- **The 2025 guidance was cut, twice in effect.** In May 2025 management lowered the outlook, attributing it to supply constraints from the China exit. In August 2025 they cut again, this time on US drinkware market conditions. An analyst (Anna Glaessgen, May 2025) pressed exactly on this: "It feels like the majority of the sales reduction is related to a lack of inventory to be able to meet underlying demand." They said drinkware would "return to growth starting in Q4" (said in August 2025) — drinkware grew 6% in the fourth quarter and 5% in the first quarter of 2026. - **The beat rate corroborates.** Seven of seven quarters beaten on earnings. The most recent: $0.26 adjusted against a $0.18 consensus in the first quarter of 2026 — a 47% beat, which is a wide enough margin to suggest deliberately conservative guidance.

**Sandbagging pattern: yes, and it is now visible.** A 100% beat rate with beats of that size means the guidance floor is set low. Investors should read the published range as a floor, not a midpoint. The qualification on the score is that sandbagging cuts both ways — the same conservatism means the 2026 raise to $2.83–$2.89 of adjusted earnings may itself be beatable, which is the bull's strongest structural argument.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The category definition keeps widening, and that is a tell in both directions.** Drinkware was tumblers; by February 2026 it was "4 platforms: bottles and jugs, cups, mugs and tumblers, tableware, coffeeware, barware and containers; and finally, cookware." A company that redefines a category while that category is flat is managing the optics of a comparison. It is also, in this case, genuinely entering adjacent markets — the shaker bottle, the cast-iron pan, the ceramic mugs are real products with real reviews. Read it as both.

**"Inorganic innovation" is the new phrase for buying things.** Reintjes was careful in November 2025: "it's not tuck-in in the traditional sense of the tuck-in of a business or a brand, it's really about access to capabilities." The company bought Mystery Ranch (2024), Butter Pat, the Helimix shaker design and tooling (2025), and a cast-iron design. Helimix "will cease operations as we relaunch an updated design." This is acquisition-led product development described as internal innovation. It is not deceptive — the calls disclose each deal — but it does mean the organic innovation engine is being supplemented more than the language admits.

**A new voice with a different vocabulary.** Scott Bomar, in his first quarter as finance chief (May 2026), speaks in terms of "the earnings power of the model," "structural margin drivers of mix, sourcing and pricing," and half-by-half margin bridges. McMullen spoke in terms of working capital, safety stock and inventory levels. The finance function has been repositioned from defence to narrative — worth watching, because the same person now owns the guidance that the sandbagging pattern rests on.

**Competition is discussed only obliquely.** Across five calls, no competitor is ever named. The promotional pressure is always "the market," "some brands out there," "certain trend-driven styles." A brand that took heavy share losses in insulated drinkware during 2023–2024 has chosen never to say from whom.

**Capital-allocation language shifted from defence to conviction.** August 2025: "we want to make sure we maintain a really strong balance sheet." November 2025: buybacks "show the conviction we have in what we're doing at YETI." That is a management team that believes its own stock was cheap — and it was, at the prices they bought.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory classification: STRENGTHENING.**

The operating turn is real and is corroborated by the numbers, not just the narrative: drinkware has grown for two consecutive quarters after a year of decline, wholesale posted its best quarter in three years, international is compounding above 20%, the China exit is complete and ahead of schedule, and guidance was raised in May 2026 rather than trimmed. Cash generation exceeds reported profit, and roughly 8% of the company has been retired in a year.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *the seven-and-a-half percentage points of revenue that have migrated into operating costs since 2021 have not yet produced a single dollar of incremental profit.* Gross margin is flat at 57%, so the brand is not the problem — the spending is. Five design offices, a 400-million-impression campaign, an artificial-intelligence shopping assistant, a Japan build-out and a series of design acquisitions are all being funded out of the operating line, and management has never given a date or a number for when that spend converts to margin. The bull case and the bear case both turn entirely on this one question, and the stock is priced as though the answer is already known. At $50.72 the market pays roughly 17.7 times the midpoint of guided 2026 adjusted earnings and 3.6 times trailing gross profit for a business whose earnings per share are lower than they were five years ago.

**Economic moat: NARROW, of the intangible-brand type.**

The evidence for a moat is the gross margin — 57%, essentially unchanged since 2021, defended through a tariff shock and a promotional war, with brand awareness, consideration and preference all at or near record levels and product satisfaction around 98%. Customers pay a premium and keep paying it. That is a real, measurable brand asset.

The evidence against calling it wide is equally clear. Insulated drinkware has almost no barrier to entry, and YETI lost meaningful share to newer entrants during 2023 and 2024 — the "cleanup" and "trend-driven styles" language across four consecutive calls is management describing a category where consumer preference moves faster than the moat can defend. There are no switching costs, no network effects and no regulatory protection. The coolers and bags franchise is sturdier — heritage, price-ladder coverage from the $50–$150 Daytrip up to the $200–$350 line, and genuine product reputation — but it is a product moat, not a structural one.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Returns have fallen — return on invested capital of roughly 16.6% on a trailing basis against about 20% two years ago, and operating margin from 14.5% to 10.8% — which would normally read as erosion. But the compression is entirely below the gross-profit line, and gross margin is the metric that measures competitive position. Falling returns caused by deliberate investment and a tariff regime are a capital-allocation question, not a moat question. If the gross margin ever breaks below the mid-fifties, this rating should move immediately to eroding.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** No structural force is dismantling the terminal value here. The e-commerce channel shift, which impairs mall-based retail and wholesale distributors, works *for* YETI, which sells direct through its own site, Amazon, a new TikTok shop and its own stores while wholesale reaccelerates. There is no artificial-intelligence displacement risk, no reimbursement or regulatory cliff, no energy-transition exposure. The genuine risk is cyclical and category-fashion in nature: insulated drinkware is subject to consumer trend cycles, and a discretionary premium-priced product is exposed to a weak consumer. That is a cyclical risk, not a terminal one.

**Therefore the cheapness question is moot rather than answered: there is no cheapness to classify.** This is not a fear-print and it is not a structurally shrinking base. It is a good business, correctly recognised as such by a market that has bid it to a 52-week high, trading at approximately fair value with the profit-conversion question still open.
